name: Sara Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Sara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage a team of five in HR operations at the head office of a big hotel group. We handle all the hiring paperwork for about forty hotels: booking interviews, sending contracts, checking right-to-work documents, setting up new starters on payroll. In summer that's six hundred new people in two months, so it's a lot of spreadsheets and a lot of phone calls with hotel managers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's concrete, a person gets a job and a contract because we did it right. What wears me out is hotel managers who send everything at five on a Friday. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy up job adverts, which my colleagues showed me, but I don't rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool, not a revolution. At work I'd say let's use it for job ads and leave the rest. I might post something mild, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be quite relieved. My job's steady, my pay is normal for the role, and other hotel and retail groups in the city hire people like me. I'd just carry on saving for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, really. I'd keep putting three hundred a month toward a flat deposit, which I've done for two years. Maybe I'd ask for the contract templates to be automated, because that would save my team a day a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A normal few years is all I want right now, so I'd carry on saving for a flat by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the deposit for, and when do you hope to get there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to have the deposit in about three years, so maybe by thirty. A small one-bedroom near the river, nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel secure in your job right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty secure, yes. We get busier every summer, not quieter. The only thing that would really shake me is the group being sold, which happens in hotels, but nobody's said anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have to be sensible about it and train people up. At work I'd say let's try the tools properly, but keep a person checking the contracts. Online I'd stay out of the arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my team's work is almost all booking, checking and writing, which is the list. I think five people becomes two in a couple of years, and an HR ops manager for two people gets folded into someone else's job. So yes, my role could go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly comfortable with the AI tools once a couple of other teams had tried them. I'd ask about moving into hotel operations, like an assistant manager at one of the city hotels, where it's guests and staff on the floor. I'd keep the deposit savings going, but slower, and keep more in easy access.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a plan, so not panicking, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a route into hotel operations from head office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, there's a business course the group runs for future hotel managers, about a year part-time. I'd apply in the first round. It's less money at first, but it's a ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about the move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Marco. He's a chef at one of our hotels, and kitchens change slowly. He'd tell me to come over to the hotel side, which he's been saying for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody is ready, and companies and governments need to slow it down and help people move. At work I'd say what everyone's thinking, that head office is basically a building full of paperwork, and that's the first thing to go. Online I'd probably share a few things, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my whole job goes within two years. Every HR ops team in the country goes at the same time, so there's nowhere to move sideways. The hotels still need people on the floor until the robots come three years later, so that's where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the deposit and put everything into an emergency fund, aiming for eight months. I'd apply straight away for assistant manager jobs at our hotels, even with a pay cut. I'd talk to Marco about sharing a flat for a while to halve my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the ground had gone soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still be there in hotels in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Front desk and housekeeping supervisors are mostly people work, so those last until about 2031. After that I really don't know. Three years is a breather, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gives first in your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit. I'd hate it, but I'd rather have a year of rent safe than a flat I can't pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, so companies should start retraining people now. At work I'd push for the hotel manager course to take more head office people. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk job ends around 2031. Five years gives me time to get into hotel operations properly, not as a panic move. I'd be thirty-two with some floor experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the hotel manager course in the first year and learn the AI tools in my current job meanwhile. I'd keep saving, but split it between the deposit and an emergency pot. Around year two or three I'd move to a hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I was doing the right things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a flat in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, but I'd wait. A mortgage in 2030 on a hotel manager's starting pay is a big bet. I'd rather rent a bit longer and keep the money flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots coming three years after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housekeeping and kitchens get the robots around 2034 in this one. So the hotel job I move to would change again after a few years. I'd want to be managing people by then, not tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good amount of time if people use it. At work I'd say let's plan the next ten years properly. I wouldn't be very loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right. I'd have years in head office, then a move to hotel operations, and by 2036 I'd be a hotel manager with real people skills. The paperwork goes, but someone still runs the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job for three or four years and get good at the AI tools. Then I'd do the hotel manager course and move across around year four. I'd buy the flat by thirty, because ten years is enough to plan a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the background. Mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you sure hotels still need managers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hotels will always need someone to calm down an angry wedding party. Robots come in 2039 in this picture. By then I'd be the one deciding how to use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum, probably. She works in a bank call centre, and that's thinking work in this story. She'd be fifty-nine by 2036, and that's a hard age to start again.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It takes my job and my flat plan at the same time. What would help is companies paying for people to retrain into the hands-on side, and some notice, like a year, before they close a team.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the people we hire. If HR is all software, who notices when a nineteen-year-old on a zero-hours contract is being treated badly? That's a real part of my job that nobody counts.

headlineQuote: If HR is all software, who notices when a nineteen-year-old on a zero-hours contract is being treated badly?
portrait: Sara, 27, runs a **five-person** HR operations team for a hotel group and lives alone, renting.
She is saving for a **flat deposit** and uses AI tools now and then.
Pragmatic and centrist, she wants companies to **train people** rather than just cut.
She is calm in AI Plateau, then sees her **desk job** going in every faster picture.
Her route is **hotel operations**, with her brother Marco, a chef, urging her across.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, which takes her **job and flat plan** together.
whatWouldHelp: A year's **notice** before a team is closed.
